lead: Network categories group communication systems by how far they stretch. A LAN stays inside a single building, a MAN covers a city or campus, and a WAN spans a country or the world. The idea helps engineers pick the right technology, budget, and management style for the area they must serve. These categories appear when a college builds its internal network, when Chennai Metro runs a city‑wide fiber ring, or when a bank links branches across India.
prereq: You need: basics of data communication from Chapter 1.1.

blocks.text: A Local Area Network (LAN) connects devices that are in one building or a tightly bounded area such as a college department. LANs use Ethernet cables or Wi‑Fi and typically provide speeds from 100 Mbps to 10 Gbps. A Metropolitan Area Network (MAN) links several LANs across a city. MANs often use fiber‑optic links and support 1 Gbps to 100 Gbps. A Wide Area Network (WAN) joins LANs or MANs that are far apart, possibly across countries. WANs use leased lines, satellite links, or the public Internet and may offer 10 Mbps to several hundred Gbps.

items: Campus LAN – Ethernet inside a university building.
Chennai Metro MAN – 10 Gbps fiber ring connecting stations.
National bank WAN – leased MPLS circuits linking branches.

blocks.text: Some syllabi call these three groups "network categories" because they share similar design goals and constraints. The larger the area, the higher the cost per kilometre of link and the more complex the routing.

LANs usually run Ethernet. A common campus LAN uses 1 Gbps full‑duplex copper or fiber. The technology cost is low and installation is easy. MANs often adopt dense wavelength division multiplexing (DWDM) fiber. A city MAN may be provisioned for 10 Gbps or more, allowing many LANs to share the backbone. WANs rely on leased lines or MPLS. A banking WAN might have a 100 Mbps leased line per branch, but the aggregate capacity of the backbone can be many gigabits.

blocks.where: B₁, B₂, B₃ are the individual link capacities (in the same unit).

blocks.text: If a college LAN (1 Gbps), a city MAN (10 Gbps), and a bank WAN (100 Mbps) are all used together, the total usable bandwidth is 1 Gbps + 10 Gbps + 0.1 Gbps = 11.1 Gbps.
Understanding these numbers helps when you later study routing in Chapter 1.8.

Design decisions differ for each category. LAN design focuses on low latency and high throughput within a short distance. MAN design balances cost of fiber deployment with the need to serve many organisations. WAN design must handle long distances, variable latency, and often uses protocols that tolerate loss, such as TCP over satellite links.

items: Cost per kilometre rises from LAN to WAN.
Management complexity grows with area size.
Choice of physical media (copper, fiber, radio) follows the category.

blocks.text: Later chapters on topologies, protocols, and devices will refer back to these categories when explaining why a star LAN uses a switch, why a ring MAN may use a ring topology such as SONET/SDH rings, and why a WAN needs routers.

figure.caption: Nested sets show that a LAN is contained inside a MAN, which in turn is contained inside a WAN.

spec.aria: Nested sets illustrate that LANs are inside MANs which are inside WANs.

examples.question: A college has a LAN with 1 Gbps Ethernet. The city MAN that connects the college to other campuses provides 10 Gbps fiber. The bank that hosts the college’s financial services offers a 100 Mbps leased line WAN. If these three links are independent parallel connections, what is the total aggregate bandwidth available to the college?
steps: Convert all capacities to the same unit. 1 Gbps = 1 Gbps, 10 Gbps = 10 Gbps, 100 Mbps = 0.1 Gbps.
Add the three values: 1 Gbps + 10 Gbps + 0.1 Gbps = 11.1 Gbps.
examples.answer: The total aggregate bandwidth is 11.1 Gbps.

traps: Confusing the coverage area: a LAN does NOT span a whole city; that is a MAN.
Adding bandwidths without converting units: mixing Mbps and Gbps gives a wrong total.
Assuming a MAN is always faster than a WAN; speed depends on the specific technology, not the category.
Thinking that a WAN always uses satellite links; many WANs use fiber or leased lines.

quiz.q: Explain why a MAN typically uses fiber optics while a LAN can use copper cables.
quiz.a: MAN covers larger distances where signal attenuation in copper becomes a problem; fiber offers lower loss and higher bandwidth over kilometres. LAN distances are short, so copper is cheaper and sufficient.

quiz.q: A company has three sites: two LANs each with 1 Gbps and a WAN link of 200 Mbps connecting them. Compute the total bandwidth the company can use simultaneously.
quiz.a: Convert 200 Mbps to 0.2 Gbps. Total = 1 Gbps + 1 Gbps + 0.2 Gbps = 2.2 Gbps.

quiz.q: If a city upgrades its MAN from 10 Gbps to 40 Gbps, discuss two impacts on the LANs that connect to it.
quiz.a: 1) LANs can experience higher aggregate throughput when multiple LANs send traffic simultaneously, reducing congestion. 2) The upgrade may justify investing in faster LAN equipment (e.g., 10 Gbps Ethernet) to avoid creating a new bottleneck at the LAN‑MAN interface.

quiz.q: Which category typically spans a whole country or the globe?
A university campus has a LAN of 1 Gbps and a MAN of 5 Gbps. If a video stream requires 3 Gbps, can it be carried without congestion? Justify.
quiz.a: The LAN alone cannot support 3 Gbps (its limit is 1 Gbps). Even though the MAN has enough capacity, the bottleneck is the LAN, so the stream would be congested.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, the rise of edge computing blurs the line between LAN and MAN as processing moves closer to users. Research on software‑defined wide area networking (SD‑WAN) lets enterprises program WAN behaviour dynamically. Future curricula add cloud‑native networking where virtual LANs span multiple data‑center locations. To explore further, search for "SD‑WAN architectures" and "edge computing network design".
